strengths: Novel theoretical contribution connecting differential privacy sensitivity to Jacobi fields and manifold curvature through careful application of the Rauch comparison theorem
Mathematically rigorous derivations with sound proofs of sensitivity bounds for both footpoint (Theorem 3.4) and shooting vector parameters
General framework applicable to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds, addressing an important and understudied problem at the intersection of differential geometry and differential privacy
Empirical validation of theoretical sensitivity bounds (Figure 5) showing tightness with 3-4x factors, confirming theoretical predictions

weaknesses: Severely limited experimental evaluation: only 20 synthetic points on sphere and 100-row Wine dataset; no experiments on other manifolds despite claiming applicability to shape spaces and SPD matrices; no privacy-utility tradeoff analysis or real applications demonstrated

Restrictive and underexplored assumptions: τ-closeness requirement may not hold in practice; no guidance on verification or violation; implications of bounded data assumption not discussed
Loose sensitivity bounds: empirically 3-4× loose (Figure 5); dependence on maximum error τ could be pessimistic; sensitivity inflation for positively curved manifolds mentioned but not quantified

Weak baseline comparisons: single Wine dataset configuration for linear regression; IBM Diffprivlib performs poorly (7.856 vs 0.954 MSE) but no root cause analysis; missing comparisons with other cited DP linear regression methods across varying privacy budgets and dataset sizes

Limited methodological novelty: primarily applies existing Soto et al. [2022] KNG mechanism to geodesic regression; Jacobi field approach inspired by Reimherr et al. [2021]; incremental contribution over prior work

Significant practical implementation gaps: no code provided; choosing τ in practice unclear; no complexity analysis; dimension scaling behavior not studied; MCMC hyperparameter choices (η ∝ σ) not justified

Presentation issues: Figures 2-3 difficult to read; intuition for Jacobi field connection insufficient; critical sampling procedure relegated to appendix; heavy notation without adequate intuitive explanation

strengths: Addresses novel and timely problem of extending differential privacy to geodesic regression on Riemannian manifolds
Derives theoretically sound sensitivity bounds (Lemma 3.3, Theorem 3.4) with elegant connection to Jacobi fields and manifold curvature via Rauch comparison theorem
Provides rigorous mathematical foundations with comprehensive background on Riemannian geometry and differential privacy
Demonstrates theoretical correctness by verifying special case (Euclidean space) reduces to linear regression and validates sensitivity bounds via empirical ratios
Framework is general and could potentially apply to diverse manifolds (symmetric positive definite matrices, shape spaces, etc.)
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: sphere experiments use only 20 synthetic points, linear regression tests on 100-row wine dataset; no experiments on actual manifold-valued response data despite being the paper's main contribution
No systematic privacy-utility analysis: only ε=2 evaluated; missing studies across multiple privacy budgets and dataset sizes critical for differential privacy work

Restrictive and unjustified assumptions: Assumption 3.2 requires data in ball of radius r ≤ π/(8√κ) (≈0.39 radians for unit sphere)—extremely limiting; τ-closeness condition's practical feasibility never discussed
Critical gap in practical applicability: τ (maximum error magnitude) must be specified a priori; if estimated from data, DP guarantees are violated; no guidance on τ selection

Severe computational limitations: requires MCMC sampling acknowledged as difficult; Figure 6 reports only 11 replicates at large n due to computational burden; Jacobi field computation tractable only for constant-curvature manifolds

Inconsistent experimental methodology: non-standard evaluation protocol (40,000 parameter pairs vs. single true parameters); mixing of metrics (squared geodesic distance vs. MAE); weak baselines missing recent methods like Alabi et al. 2020

All demonstrated results limited to constant-curvature manifolds (sphere, Euclidean); promised applications (medical imaging, Kendall shape space, computer vision) mentioned in introduction but completely unvalidated
Weak utility improvements: DPGR (MSE=0.954) vs. OPACUS (MSE=0.982) shows only ~3% difference; no formal utility guarantees or estimation error bounds provided

Gaps in theoretical analysis: sensitivity bounds are data-dependent requiring Jacobi field initial conditions; Theorem 3.4 introduces looseness (mean ratio r_p=3.12, r_v=3.92); behavior of shooting vector sensitivities poorly explained

Missing reproducibility details: no code availability; MCMC implementation incomplete (η tuning specified only as 'proportional to σ'); no convergence diagnostics or numerical methods for solving Jacobi equations discussed
Presentation issues: redundant sections (2.2 repeated), Figure 1 appears twice, lacking intuitive explanation of Jacobi field connection before technical proofs

strengths: Elegant theoretical contribution: Sensitivity bounds tied to Jacobi fields and manifold curvature via Rauch comparison theorem provide novel insights connecting differential geometry to privacy
Rigorous mathematical framework: Proofs are sound and sophisticated differential geometry is correctly applied; theoretical development is complete and detailed
Generality to Riemannian manifolds: Methodology applies to any manifold with bounded sectional curvature; unifies geodesic and linear regression under single DP framework
Excellent mathematical exposition: Background section clearly presents necessary Riemannian geometry; appendices provide comprehensive proofs and details
Theoretical validation: Appendix B empirically validates sensitivity bounds are tight (not vacuous), with theoretical bounds 3-4x loose relative to empirical values
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: Only S² evaluated despite claimed generality to all Riemannian manifolds; no experiments on SPD matrices, Kendall shape space, or other mentioned applications; synthetic experiments use only 20 data points; single real dataset with 100 rows insufficient

Suspicious experimental results: DPGR achieves ~85x better MSE than IBM Diffprivlib under same privacy budget (0.954 vs 7.856) without adequate explanation; raises questions about fair comparison, hyperparameter tuning, or privacy budget allocation

Practical implementation challenges inadequately addressed: Sampling from KNG requires Metropolis-Hastings with manifold random walk; requires tuning parameter η with no selection guidance; paper acknowledges sampling difficulty but defers to future work; no computational complexity or scalability analysis

Restrictive and under-discussed assumptions: Assumption 3.2 requires data in ball of radius π/(8√κ) for positive curvature; τ-closeness requirement; practical implications and applicability to real data not thoroughly discussed

Missing utility-privacy tradeoff analysis: No finite-sample convergence rates or sample complexity as function of ε and n; no guidance on privacy budget allocation between footpoint and shooting vector; sensitivity still data-dependent via τ despite Rauch comparison

Incomplete practical guidance: No methods for setting τ a priori; no justification for ε parameter choices in experiments; no discussion of privacy budget selection strategies for practitioners; composition tradeoff for combined (p,v) privacy budgets unexplored

Limited related work discussion: Connection to Reimherr et al. [2021] on DP Fréchet means mentioned but not deeply analyzed; no comparison of utility-privacy tradeoffs with alternative approaches; unclear when geodesic regression is preferable to alternatives

Computational scalability concerns: Appendix B notes sampling 'requires significantly extended computational duration' for n > 20; only 11 replicates evaluated at n=35; no scalability demonstrated to realistic problem sizes

Limited experimental validation: no baseline comparisons (acknowledged), experiments mostly illustrate expected behavior without novel insights; no error bars, MCMC diagnostics, or timing analysis

Absence of code release and no discussion of computational efficiency or scalability despite claiming general framework

strengths: Novel first study of differential privacy for geodesic regression with theoretically rigorous sensitivity bounds that elegantly connect to Jacobi fields and manifold curvature
Sound mathematical analysis: Proper application of Rauch comparison theorem and differential geometry; proofs are careful and well-structured
General methodology applicable to any Riemannian manifold with bounded curvature, enabling applications across multiple domains (medical imaging, computer vision, shape analysis)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple manifolds (sphere, SPD matrices, Kendall shape space) with varying data sizes and privacy budget allocations
Empirical validation of theoretical bounds in Appendix G shows sensitivities are both valid and tight through systematic testing on adjacent datasets
Clear and thorough presentation with extensive background material; honest discussion of limitations rather than obscuring them
weaknesses: Critical gap between theory and practice: Implementation requires setting τ = max_i ||ε_i|| from data, which violates differential privacy, while theory assumes τ = sup_i ||ε_i||. The proposed mitigation via 'public information' is vague and domain-specific, leaving this fundamental limitation inadequately addressed
MCMC sampling introduces approximate differential privacy (δ = O(1/M)), converting pure DP to approximate DP and reducing theoretical elegance; adequate chains could require prohibitive computation
No baseline comparisons to evaluate utility-privacy tradeoffs relative to alternative approaches; authors discuss why alternatives are non-trivial but provide no empirical comparison

Limited experimental scope: small datasets (20-100 points), primarily synthetic/semi-synthetic data, no statistical significance testing, no error bars, no sensitivity analysis on parameter choices (e.g., how results depend on τ)

Practical concerns with curvature-dependent sensitivity: For negatively curved spaces, sensitivity involves exponential terms cosh(2√-κ_l(τ_m+τ)) that could be prohibitively large for highly curved manifolds, deserving more discussion

Presentation and reproducibility gaps: Dense notation limits accessibility, no pseudocode provided, MCMC hyperparameters incompletely specified, no code release mentioned, computation of Jacobi fields per-manifold underdocumented
